prompt: A service writes a log file while the machine is running. Which directory is it under?
hint: One of these holds what changes; the others hold what was installed or configured.

choices.text: /etc
choices.why: Configuration lives here. It is read while running, and rarely written.

choices.text: /usr
choices.why: Installed programs and their data. A package manager writes here; a service does not.

choices.text: /var
choices.why: Right. Logs, spools and working data — what the machine writes as it runs.

choices.text: /opt
choices.why: Software placed outside the package manager. Its logs still belong in /var.

prompt: `ls -ld /bin` prints a line beginning with `l` and ending `-> usr/bin`. What is `/bin` on this machine?
hint: The first character of a long listing is the type.

choices.text: A symbolic link into /usr
choices.why: Yes — the usr merge. /bin/ls and /usr/bin/ls are one file with two paths.

choices.text: An empty directory
choices.why: An empty directory would list as `d` with nothing after the name.

choices.text: A directory mounted from another disk
choices.why: A mount point lists as an ordinary directory. This line says `l`.

choices.text: A broken entry left by a failed upgrade
choices.why: It resolves fine. The arrow is how a working symlink is drawn.

prompt: You compile a tool from source and install it by hand. Where does it belong, so the package manager leaves it alone?
hint: There is a directory reserved for exactly this, one level inside another.

choices.text: /bin
choices.why: That is the system's own commands, managed by packages.

choices.text: /home/you/bin
choices.why: Fine for you alone, and invisible to everybody else on the machine.

choices.text: /var/local
choices.why: This exists, and it holds variable data rather than programs.

choices.text: /usr/local
choices.why: Right — reserved for software installed by hand, and untouched by packages.

prompt: A program needs a scratch file that has to survive a reboot. `/tmp` or `/var/tmp`?
hint: Both are scratch. They differ in how long the scratch lives.

choices.text: /tmp, because scratch files belong there by convention
choices.why: By convention /tmp is wiped at boot, which is the one thing this file has to survive.

choices.text: /var/tmp, which is not cleared at boot
choices.why: Right. That is the difference between the two, and the reason both exist.

choices.text: Either — the two directories behave the same way
choices.why: They are both scratch, and their lifetimes differ. That difference is the whole point.

choices.text: Neither; a file like that belongs in /run
choices.why: /run is cleared at boot too, and it is for sockets and PIDs rather than data.

prompt: Match each directory to what is kept in it.
hint: Four of these you will open by hand; the distractors describe other directories.

pairs.right: what the machine wrote while running
the kernel and its processes, as files

right_distractors: the kernel image and the bootloader

prompt: Which of these is an absolute path?
hint: One character at the front decides it.

choices.text: work/src/main.c
choices.why: No leading slash, so it starts from wherever you happen to be.

choices.text: /home/ana/work
choices.why: Yes. It starts at the root, so it means the same thing typed anywhere.

choices.text: ../src/main.c
choices.why: It starts by going up from here, which makes it relative.

choices.text: ./ledger
choices.why: The leading dot is 'here', so this one depends on where here is.

prompt: A cron job runs `tar -czf backup.tar.gz logs/`. It succeeds every night and the backups are nowhere to be found. Why?
hint: A scheduled job does not start in the directory you wrote the line in.

choices.text: cron strips relative paths out of the command before running it
choices.why: cron passes the line through. It changes where the line runs, not what it says.

choices.text: tar refuses relative paths and writes to a temporary directory instead
choices.why: tar is happy with relative paths, and writes exactly where it was pointed.

choices.text: Both paths are relative, and cron starts the job somewhere else
choices.why: Right. The archive is being written, in a directory nobody thought to look in.

choices.text: The job runs as a different user and its writes are silently discarded
choices.why: A write it was not allowed to make would fail loudly rather than vanish.

prompt: Standing in `/home/ana/work/notes`, write the shortest relative path that reaches `/home/ana/work/src/main.c`.
hint: Up one level, then down into the sibling directory.

prompt: Why does running a program in the current directory need `./` in front of its name?
hint: It is about where the shell looks for a bare word, not about the file.

choices.text: `.` is absent from $PATH, so a bare word is not looked for here
choices.why: Right, and leaving it out of $PATH is deliberate: a planted `ls` would otherwise run.

choices.text: Programs in the current directory are treated as data rather than commands
choices.why: The file is an ordinary executable. What differs is how the shell resolves the word.

choices.text: The shell needs the dot to know the file is executable
choices.why: Whether it may run is in its permission bits, which the dot has no bearing on.

choices.text: Bash wants a path separator in front of any program it is asked to start
choices.why: It starts programs by bare name constantly — that is what $PATH is for.

prompt: `ls -di / /. /..` prints the number 2 three times. What does that tell you?
hint: The number is the filesystem's own identifier for a thing.

choices.text: The root directory contains two entries
choices.why: That number is an identifier, not a count of what is inside.

choices.text: Two of the three paths are invalid
choices.why: Three inode numbers were printed, so three paths resolved.

choices.text: The root directory is two levels deep
choices.why: Depth is not what an inode number measures.

choices.text: They are three names for one directory
choices.why: Right. The root's parent is itself, so /.. is /.

prompt: `echo '~/work'` prints `~/work` rather than `/home/ana/work`. Why?
hint: Ask who was supposed to rewrite the tilde, and whether it got the chance.

choices.text: echo does not understand the tilde and prints it raw
choices.why: echo never understands it. The rewriting is the shell's job, and quotes stopped it.

choices.text: Single quotes stopped the shell from expanding it
choices.why: Right. Unquoted, the shell would have replaced it before echo ran.

choices.text: The tilde expands after the command runs, so echo prints the old text
choices.why: Expansion happens while the line is parsed, which is before anything runs.

choices.text: A tilde followed by a slash is a different shorthand with its own meaning
choices.why: `~/work` is the ordinary form. The quoting is what changed the outcome here.

prompt: You are in `/var/log`, you `cd /etc`, and then you type `cd -`. Where do you end up?
hint: The dash is a shorthand for one specific directory.

choices.why: The dash is not 'up' and not 'the root'.

choices.text: Your home directory
choices.why: That is `cd` with no argument at all.

choices.text: /var/log
choices.why: Right — the previous directory, and it prints the path as it goes.

choices.text: /etc, since the dash cancels the last cd
choices.why: It moves you, rather than undoing the move in place.

prompt: Which single command takes you to your home directory from anywhere, with no argument?
hint: Two letters.

prompt: You want the newest file in a directory of two hundred logs to be the last line printed. Which listing?
hint: Two options, and the second one reverses the first.

choices.text: ls -l --sort=size
choices.why: That sorts by size, biggest first.

choices.text: ls -la
choices.why: That adds the hidden names, and leaves the order alphabetical.

choices.text: ls -ltr
choices.why: Right: sort by time, then reverse, so the newest sits above your prompt.

choices.text: ls -lt
choices.why: That is newest first, which puts the one you want at the top of the scrollback.

prompt: `ls -l logs` printed four files. You wanted the permissions of `logs` itself. What was missing?
hint: One letter, and beginners rarely find it in the manual.

choices.text: -d
choices.why: Right. Without it, a directory argument means 'show me what is inside'.

choices.text: -a
choices.why: That adds hidden names to the listing, and still lists the contents.

choices.text: -R
choices.why: That descends further rather than stopping at the directory.

choices.text: -i
choices.why: That prints inode numbers beside whatever is already being listed.

prompt: `cd work/README.md` answers `bash: cd: work/README.md: Not a directory`. What does that message rule out?
hint: Compare it with the other two things cd says when it refuses.

choices.text: That you have permission to enter it
choices.why: A refusal about permission says `Permission denied` instead.

choices.text: That the path is wrong
choices.why: Right — the path resolved. What it reached is a file.

choices.text: That the file exists
choices.why: It does exist. That is why the complaint is about its kind.

choices.text: That bash was the one refusing
choices.why: bash is named at the front of the line, so bash is speaking.

prompt: Why does `man cd` find nothing while `help cd` works?
hint: Think about what would happen if cd were a separate program.

choices.text: cd is too small to have been given a manual page
choices.why: Size is not the reason, and plenty of tiny commands have pages.

choices.text: The manual pages for shell commands are in a package you have not installed
choices.why: Installing more manuals would still not produce one, because there is no program to document.

choices.text: man covers commands and help covers options, which is a different question
choices.why: help documents commands too — the ones built into the shell.

choices.text: cd is built into the shell, so there is no program for man to describe
choices.why: Right: a separate program changing its own directory would leave the shell where it was.

prompt: A long listing line starts with `d`. What is the entry?
hint: The first character is the type, and it is not part of the permissions.

choices.text: A device
choices.why: A device shows `c` or `b` there, depending on how it is read.

choices.text: A directory
choices.why: Yes. The nine characters after it are its permissions.

choices.text: A symbolic link
choices.why: A symlink shows `l`, and prints an arrow after the name.

choices.text: A file the owner may delete
choices.why: Deleting is decided by the directory holding the name, not by this letter.

prompt: `drwxr-xr-x 2 ana ana 4096 Mar 26 2025 logs`. What does the `2` say about `logs`?
hint: For a directory the count starts at two, and section 39 said why.

choices.text: Two files are inside it
choices.why: The count is about names pointing at the directory, not its contents.

choices.text: Two people may write to it
choices.why: Who may write is in the nine permission characters, not here.

choices.text: It holds no subdirectories
choices.why: Right: its own name plus its `.`, and a subdirectory's `..` would add one more.

choices.text: It was modified twice since it was made
choices.why: Modifications are not counted anywhere in a listing.

prompt: One `ls -l` listing shows `Mar 22  2025` on one line and `Sep 14 21:58` on another. Why the two formats?
hint: One of the two entries is much more recent than the other.

choices.text: Recent entries get a time, older ones get a year
choices.why: Right — roughly six months is the cut, and `--full-time` prints both the same way.

choices.text: Directories get a year and files get a time
choices.why: Both lines can be directories. Age is what decides the format.

choices.text: Entries on another filesystem are printed differently
choices.why: One filesystem or several, the format follows the age of the entry.

choices.text: The second entry has a timestamp the filesystem could not fully record
choices.why: Both timestamps are complete. It is the printing that is being shortened.

prompt: Four files of 440, 8, 0 and 31 bytes, and the listing opens with `total 12`. What is 12?
hint: It is not the count, and it is not the sum of the sizes.

choices.text: The number of bytes rounded to kilobytes
choices.why: 479 bytes does not round to 12 of anything.

choices.text: The number of entries, including hidden ones
choices.why: There are four entries, hidden or not.

choices.text: The size of the directory's own list of names
choices.why: That is the 4096 you see on the directory's own line.

choices.text: The 1-KiB blocks the disk gave these entries
choices.why: Right: three files took a block each, and the empty one took none.

prompt: Put the fields of a long listing in the order `ls -l` prints them.
trap: Owner comes before group, and the size comes before the date.

prompt: `cp other.txt keep.txt` runs, and `keep.txt` already existed. What happened to the old contents?
hint: Count the prompts and the warnings you saw.

choices.text: They went to a trash directory the shell keeps
choices.why: There is no such directory, and no undo behind it.

choices.text: They were kept, because cp refuses to overwrite by default
choices.why: It overwrites by default. `-i` is what makes it ask.

choices.text: They are gone, with no prompt and nothing to restore from
choices.why: Right. That silence is the deal, and it is why `ls` first is a habit.

choices.text: They were appended to, so the file now holds both
choices.why: A copy replaces the destination rather than adding to it.

prompt: `cp archive backup` prints `cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'archive'`. Is that an error?
hint: Look at what the command did with everything else it was given.

choices.text: No — it is a notice that one argument was skipped
choices.why: Right, and in a command copying twenty things it scrolls past while the rest succeed.

choices.text: Yes, and the copy stopped at that point
choices.why: It carries on with the remaining arguments, which is what makes this easy to miss.

choices.text: Yes, and the destination was left empty
choices.why: Everything that was a file did get copied. The directory is what got left.

choices.text: No — it means the directory was copied without its contents
choices.why: Nothing of the directory was copied. `omitting` is literal.

prompt: Moving a 4 GB file inside one filesystem is instant; moving it to another disk takes minutes. Why?
hint: Ask what a rename actually changes on disk.

choices.text: mv compresses the file when it crosses a disk
choices.why: It copies the bytes as they are, without compressing.

choices.text: The second disk is slower, and that is the whole difference
choices.why: Even on identical disks, crossing between them copies.

choices.text: mv checks the destination filesystem before writing
choices.why: A check would take a moment, not minutes.

choices.text: Within one filesystem it is a rename, not a copy
choices.why: Right — a rename changes which directory holds the name, and moves no data.

prompt: When does `rmdir` succeed where `rm -r` would also have worked, and tell you something `rm -r` would not?
hint: One of the two checks an assumption for you.

choices.text: When the directory lives on a filesystem you may not write to
choices.why: Neither of them can remove anything there.

choices.text: When it is empty, and a refusal tells you it is not
choices.why: Right. Use it when emptiness is the thing you believe, and let it check.

choices.text: When you lack permission on the files inside
choices.why: Then rmdir refuses too, for the same reason.

choices.text: When the directory holds a mount point beneath it
choices.why: Neither removes a directory with something mounted under it.

prompt: `rm -rf "$DIR/"` is in a script and `DIR` was never set. What does the shell hand to `rm`?
hint: Substitute the empty string and read what is left.

choices.text: An empty argument, so rm prints its usage and stops
choices.why: Something is left after the substitution, and it is a valid path.

choices.text: The literal text $DIR/, which does not exist
choices.why: Inside double quotes the variable is substituted, empty or not.

choices.text: A single slash, which is the root of the tree
choices.why: Right. GNU rm refuses that one specifically, and `set -u` is the real fix.

choices.text: The current directory, because an unset variable means here
choices.why: An unset variable expands to nothing at all, not to a dot.

prompt: Somebody hands you `data.bin`, and the extension may be a lie. Which command answers what it actually contains?
hint: One command reads the bytes and tells you what they are.

choices.text: cat data.bin
choices.why: If those bytes are binary, your terminal stops drawing text properly.

choices.text: file data.bin
choices.why: Right. It reads the first bytes and names the format, whatever the extension claims.

choices.text: wc -l data.bin
choices.why: That counts lines, which assumes an answer you do not have yet.

choices.text: stat data.bin
choices.why: That describes the entry — size, owner, dates — and says nothing about the content.

prompt: `stat` shows Modify in March and Change today. What changed today?
hint: One of the three timestamps covers more than the contents.

choices.text: The contents, and the Modify line is stale
choices.why: Modify is the contents. It would have moved.

choices.text: Somebody read the file
choices.why: Reading moves Access, and leaves Change alone.

choices.text: The file was copied somewhere else
choices.why: Copying makes a new entry; it does not touch this one.

choices.text: Its name, permissions or owner
choices.why: Right — ctime covers the metadata, and that is what this pair is telling you.

prompt: `wc logs/app.log` prints ` 30  80 440`. What are the three numbers?
hint: They are in a fixed order, and the last is the biggest for a reason.

choices.text: Lines, words, bytes
choices.why: Yes, and `-l`, `-w` or `-c` asks for one of them on its own.

choices.text: Bytes, words, lines
choices.why: The order runs the other way, from the coarsest count to the finest.

choices.text: Lines, characters, blocks
choices.why: Blocks are `du`'s subject; wc counts what is in the file.

choices.text: Words, lines, bytes
choices.why: Words come second. A file with more lines than words would be unusual.

prompt: You are watching a service fail. Which command shows each new log line as it is written?
hint: One of these stays open after it prints.

choices.text: cat /var/log/app.log
choices.why: It prints what is there and returns you to the prompt.

choices.text: head -f /var/log/app.log
choices.why: head has no such option — it works at the other end of the file.

choices.text: tail -f /var/log/app.log
choices.why: Right, and `-F` keeps following when the log is rotated overnight.

choices.text: cat /var/log/app.log | less
choices.why: It pages what exists; pressing `F` inside less is the equivalent.

prompt: You opened a pager by accident and want out. Which single key quits `less`?
hint: One letter.

prompt: Why is the pattern quoted in `find . -name '*.c'`?
hint: Two different programs could do the matching, and the quotes choose.

choices.text: Because find rejects a bare pattern and asks for quotes around it
choices.why: It takes whatever word it is handed. What differs is which word arrives.

choices.text: Because the quotes make the match case-sensitive rather than loose
choices.why: Case is `-name` against `-iname`, and quoting has no bearing on it.

choices.text: Because unquoted, the shell would expand it before find ran
choices.why: Right, and it happens to work when one such file sits in the current directory.

choices.text: Because a pattern with a dot in it would otherwise be read as a path
choices.why: A dot is an ordinary character in a filename and needs no protection.

prompt: `find . -mtime +180` — what does the plus sign do?
hint: The sign is the difference between recent and ancient.

choices.text: It selects entries older than 180 days
choices.why: Right. `-180` would select the recent ones instead.

choices.text: It selects entries changed within the last 180 days
choices.why: That is what the minus sign asks for.

choices.text: It adds 180 days to the comparison date
choices.why: The number is an age, and the sign says which side of it.

choices.text: It rounds the age up to whole days
choices.why: Days are the unit either way; the sign chooses a direction.

prompt: `find /etc -name 'hosts'` mixes `Permission denied` lines in with the result. What removes them?
hint: The complaints and the results are on two different streams.

choices.text: Adding -quiet to find
choices.why: find has no such option, and the messages are not really find's to hide.

choices.text: Running it with sudo so the complaints stop
choices.why: That works, and it is a large hammer for reading one path.

choices.text: Piping the output through grep -v denied
choices.why: The complaints are not in the output being piped, so grep never sees them.

choices.text: Appending 2>/dev/null
choices.why: Right: the errors go to stream 2, and that sends stream 2 away.

prompt: `-exec ls -lh {} +` versus `-exec ls -lh {} \;` — what is the difference?
hint: One of them starts the command once.

choices.text: The plus form keeps going after an error, the semicolon form stops
choices.why: Both carry on. What changes is how many times the command is started.

choices.text: The plus form starts the command once, with every result
choices.why: Right, and it is faster; the semicolon form is for commands taking one file.

choices.text: The semicolon form passes the results through a pipe instead
choices.why: No pipe is involved: each result is substituted for the braces.

choices.text: The plus form is a GNU extension and the semicolon form is portable
choices.why: Both are standard, and the difference between them is about batching.

prompt: `locate report.csv` returns a path that no longer exists. Is `locate` broken?
hint: Ask where locate looked.

choices.text: Yes — a stale result means the index is corrupt
choices.why: A stale result means the index is old, which is its normal condition.

choices.text: Yes — locate is supposed to check each hit before printing it
choices.why: Checking each hit would cost the speed that is the reason to use it.

choices.text: No — it reads an index, and the disk has moved on since
choices.why: Right. `updatedb` rebuilds it, and `find` is what asks the filesystem itself.

choices.text: No — it was searching a different filesystem from the one you meant
choices.why: It indexes the whole tree. Age is what separates it from the truth.

prompt: `echo *.txt` prints `a.txt b.txt`. Who decided which names came out?
hint: echo prints what it was handed. Something handed it two words.

choices.text: echo, which looks up matching names before printing them
choices.why: echo has no idea what a filename is. It printed two words it was given.

choices.text: The shell, before echo was started
choices.why: Right — that is globbing, and it happens to every command you type.

choices.text: The kernel, when echo asked it to open the pattern
choices.why: Nothing was opened. The names were substituted into the command line.

choices.text: The terminal, which rewrites patterns as it draws the line
choices.why: The terminal draws characters and sends keys, and rewrites nothing.

prompt: `ls nope*` says `ls: cannot access 'nope*': No such file or directory`. Why is there a star in the message?
hint: Something decided to leave the pattern alone.

choices.text: ls prints the pattern it was searching for
choices.why: ls searched for a name, and that name is what it printed.

choices.text: The star was escaped somewhere along the way
choices.why: Nothing escaped it. It arrived intact for a different reason.

choices.text: ls does its own matching and failed at it
choices.why: ls has never matched a pattern; the shell does that before it starts.

choices.text: An unmatched pattern is passed through
choices.why: Right, so ls was handed a filename containing a star and looked for exactly that.

prompt: In a directory holding `a.txt`, `b.txt`, `c.log` and a subdirectory `sub`, `ls *` prints two listings. Why?
hint: Work out what four words the shell handed to ls.

choices.text: One of the four arguments was a directory
choices.why: Right. `ls *` is four arguments, and listing a directory means listing inside it.

choices.text: The star matched twice and ls ran once per match
choices.why: It ran once, with four arguments. Two listings came from one of them.

choices.text: ls descends into subdirectories when given a pattern
choices.why: It descends when given `-R`. Here it was handed the subdirectory by name.

choices.text: The subdirectory was listed because its name has no extension
choices.why: Extensions mean nothing here. Being a directory is what did it.

prompt: `echo {jan,feb}-report.csv` prints two names even though neither file exists. What kind of expansion is that?
hint: One of the shell's expansions does not consult the disk.

choices.text: Globbing, with the braces acting as a character set
choices.why: A character set is `[...]`, and it matches against names that exist.

choices.text: Pathname expansion, which invents the missing entries
choices.why: Pathname expansion reports what is there; it invents nothing.

choices.text: Brace expansion, which is text generation
choices.why: Right, and that is why it is the tool for creating rather than for finding.

choices.text: Tilde expansion, in its multi-value form
choices.why: Tilde expansion turns `~` into a home directory, and takes no list.

prompt: Before `rm *.log`, you want to see exactly which names the pattern will become. Write the harmless command that prints them.
hint: Two words. Use the command that prints what it is handed.

prompt: `ln report.txt hardlink.txt`, and the link count on both lines becomes 2. What does that field count?
hint: It is not about size, and it is not about permissions.

choices.text: How many times the data has been copied
choices.why: Nothing was copied. There is one set of bytes on the disk.

choices.text: How many processes have the file open
choices.why: Open handles are real, and they are counted somewhere else entirely.

choices.text: How many names point at this inode
choices.why: Right, and `rm` on one of them takes the count back down.

choices.text: How many directories the file appears under
choices.why: Two names in one directory would also make it 2.

prompt: A symlink's line says `size 10` and its target holds four megabytes. Why 10?
hint: Ask what a symlink actually stores.

choices.text: It stores the path `report.txt`, which is ten characters
choices.why: Right — a symlink is a tiny file whose contents are a path.

choices.text: It stores a ten-byte reference to the target's inode
choices.why: That would be a hard link, and a hard link has no size of its own.

choices.text: Sizes of symlinks are rounded down to the nearest ten
choices.why: Nothing rounds them. The number is the length of the stored text.

choices.text: It stores the first ten bytes of the target as a preview
choices.why: It holds no part of the target's contents, which is why it can dangle.

prompt: You delete a file that has two hard links. What has happened to the data?
hint: `unlink` is the system call, and its name is honest.

choices.text: It is queued for removal when the filesystem next runs its cleanup
choices.why: There is no such queue. The count is checked at the moment the name goes.

choices.text: It is gone, and the second name now dangles
choices.why: A dangling name is what a symlink leaves. A hard link is the file itself.

choices.text: Half of it was freed, in proportion to the names removed
choices.why: Bytes are not shared out among names like that.

choices.text: It is still there, reachable through the other name
choices.why: Right: one name went, the count dropped to 1, and the bytes stayed put.

prompt: Why can a symlink point at a directory on another disk while a hard link cannot?
hint: One of the two is written as a path and the other as a number.

choices.text: Symlinks are resolved by the shell, which sees the whole tree
choices.why: The kernel resolves both. What differs is what each one holds.

choices.text: An inode number means nothing outside its filesystem
choices.why: Right, and the loop a hard-linked directory would allow is the other half of the answer.

choices.text: Hard links are a feature of ext4 and other filesystems lack them
choices.why: Nearly every Linux filesystem has them. The restriction is about meaning, not support.

choices.text: A hard link would have to copy the directory to the second disk
choices.why: It copies nothing. It is a second name, which is why it has to stay local.

prompt: Match each command to what it prints for `rel.txt -> ../soft/report.txt`.
hint: One prints the stored text, one follows the chain to the end.

pairs.right: a line of type l, with the arrow
the contents of what it points at

right_distractors: the inode number of the link itself
an error, because the path is relative

prompt: `df -h /` prints `/dev/vda` on the left and `/` on the right. What are those two things?
hint: One is hardware and one is a directory.

choices.text: Two names the system keeps for the same disk
choices.why: One of them is a place in the tree, and places are not disks.

choices.text: The disk and the partition on it
choices.why: Both would be under /dev. The right-hand column is somewhere else.

choices.text: The device, and where it was attached
choices.why: Right — that attachment is what mounting is.

choices.text: The device, and the filesystem type on it
choices.why: The type is a separate column, and it says ext4 or similar.

prompt: A nightly backup has been writing to `/mnt/backups` for months. The disk that belongs there was never mounted. What happened?
hint: Nothing refused the write. Ask which filesystem received it.

choices.text: The backups went onto the root filesystem, filling it quietly
choices.why: Right, and it is found on the day somebody needs a backup.

choices.text: The job failed each night with a permission error
choices.why: An unmounted mount point is an ordinary directory, and writing to it works.

choices.text: The files were written and then discarded at the next boot
choices.why: /mnt is not cleared at boot. The files are sitting there.

choices.text: The data went to the disk anyway, because the kernel resolves the device
choices.why: The kernel writes where the path leads, and the path led to the main disk.

prompt: `umount /mnt/backups` says `target is busy`, and your prompt reads `root@vm:/mnt/backups#`. What is holding it?
hint: Read the prompt.

choices.text: A background job left over from whatever you ran last
choices.why: Possible in general, and the prompt names something simpler.

choices.text: Your own shell, sitting inside it
choices.why: Right. A shell sitting in a filesystem is using it; `cd /` and try again.

choices.text: The kernel, which has not finished flushing writes
choices.why: Unwritten data delays an unmount briefly, and does not report it this way.

choices.text: The mount itself, because loop devices stay busy
choices.why: A loop device unmounts like any other once nothing is using it.

prompt: Why does `/etc/fstab` name a UUID instead of `/dev/sdb1`?
hint: Think about what happens when somebody adds a second drive.

choices.text: A UUID is shorter to type than a path beginning with /dev
choices.why: It is far longer, and typing is not what fstab is for.

choices.text: Device paths under /dev are readable by root alone
choices.why: They are listed by anybody; what changes is who may open them.

choices.text: A UUID lets several disks be mounted at one point
choices.why: One filesystem per mount point either way.

choices.text: Device letters move when the disks do
choices.why: Right: the UUID belongs to the filesystem, so it survives a new cable or a new disk.

prompt: You edited `/etc/fstab` and want to rehearse it without rebooting. Write the command that mounts everything in the file that is not mounted yet.
hint: Three words, and it needs root.

prompt: A disk is full. Which command tells you which directory is responsible?
hint: One asks the filesystem how full it is; the other adds up files.

choices.text: df -h, run on the path in question
choices.why: That tells you the filesystem is full, which you already knew.

choices.text: du -sh * | sort -h
choices.why: Right, and then cd into the biggest and repeat until you arrive.

choices.text: ls -lSh, run at the top of the tree
choices.why: That sorts what is in one directory, and ignores everything below it.

choices.text: stat on the mount point
choices.why: That describes one entry, and says nothing about the tree under it.

prompt: `ls -l` says 440 bytes and `du -sh` says 4.0K for the same file. Which is wrong?
hint: They are measuring two different things.

choices.text: du, which rounds a figure up to the next kilobyte
choices.why: It reports whole blocks because whole blocks were handed out.

choices.text: ls, which is reading a stale size from the directory
choices.why: The size in the inode is current; du is reporting something else.

choices.text: du, unless the file is sparse
choices.why: Sparseness makes du report less, not more.

choices.text: Neither — one counts content, one counts disk
choices.why: Right: a block is 4 KiB here, and a file gets whole ones.

prompt: `du` reports 24K and `df` reports 31M used, on the same filesystem, at the same moment. What is going on?
hint: Something is still holding a reference that has no name.

choices.text: A deleted file is still open in a running process
choices.why: Right, and `lsof` prints it with `(deleted)` beside the name.

choices.text: df is reporting the size before compression was applied
choices.why: ext4 is not compressing anything here, and du would see the same bytes.

choices.text: du skipped a directory it lacked permission to read
choices.why: That does happen, and here du walked the whole tree as root.

choices.text: The filesystem has not flushed its writes yet
choices.why: Flushing would move both figures the same way, moments apart.

prompt: A service is writing to a log that has filled the disk. You want the space back without restarting it. What do you do?
hint: Removing the name does not remove the data while the file is open.

choices.text: rm the log, then wait for the filesystem to catch up
choices.why: The space comes back when the process closes it, which it has no reason to do.

choices.text: mv the log aside so the service writes a fresh one
choices.why: It keeps writing to the same open file, now under a different name.

choices.text: Truncate it in place with `: > /var/log/huge.log`
choices.why: Right: the file stays open, the blocks are freed, and the service carries on.

choices.text: Delete it and create an empty file with the same name
choices.why: The new name is a new inode; the old one stays open and still holds the blocks.

prompt: `df -h` shows 4% used and a program reports `No space left on device`. What do you check next?
hint: Bytes are one of the two things a filesystem runs out of.

choices.text: df -h on a different mount point
choices.why: Worth doing, and the program named a path you can already check.

choices.text: df -i, for the inode count
choices.why: Right: millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes with the disk nearly empty.

choices.text: du -sh / to find the large directory
choices.why: There is no large directory; 4% is the honest figure for bytes.

choices.text: The program's own configuration for a size limit
choices.why: Possible, and the message came from the kernel rather than the program.

prompt: What makes `.bashrc` a hidden file?
hint: It is thinner than people expect.

choices.text: Its name begins with a dot
choices.why: Right — rename it and it stops being hidden, with nothing else to change.

choices.text: A hidden bit is set in its inode
choices.why: There is no such bit in a Linux filesystem.

choices.text: It is owned by root, so ls leaves it out for you
choices.why: Ownership changes who may read it, and not whether it is listed.

choices.text: It lives in a directory that ls treats as private
choices.why: It sits in your home beside files that are listed normally.

prompt: `ls -l /proc/uptime` says 0 bytes, and `wc -c /proc/uptime` reads 16. Which one is lying?
hint: Ask where the content was, before you asked for it.

choices.text: ls, which has no way to measure a generated entry
choices.why: It measured what it was told: the kernel answered zero.

choices.text: wc, which counted the newline and its own buffer
choices.why: It counted bytes it genuinely read.

choices.text: Both, since the file is a symlink to somewhere else
choices.why: It is a regular entry in a generated filesystem, and not a link.

choices.text: Neither — the kernel makes it up on the spot
choices.why: Right. There is no stored content to have a size until a read happens.

prompt: `2>/dev/null` is typed at the end of commands constantly. What sits at the end of that redirect?
hint: Look at the first character of its line in `ls -l`.

choices.text: A shell keyword whose job is to suppress error messages
choices.why: The shell is redirecting a stream; the destination is a real path.

choices.text: An empty file the system truncates after each use
choices.why: It holds nothing at any point, and nothing truncates it.

choices.text: A character device that throws away what it is given
choices.why: Right, and reading from it gives you end-of-file straight away.

choices.text: A directory the kernel keeps for discarded output
choices.why: Its listing begins with `c`, which rules that out.

prompt: `ssh` refuses to use your key and complains about permissions. What is likely wrong?
hint: There is one shape that directory and its contents are supposed to have.

choices.text: The key is owned by root rather than by you
choices.why: That would be a different complaint, about ownership.

choices.text: `.ssh` or the key is readable by somebody else
choices.why: Right: the directory wants `drwx------` and the key `-rw-------`.

choices.text: The key was copied with cp instead of scp
choices.why: Either tool produces the same file; it is the mode that matters.

choices.text: `.ssh` is hidden, and ssh looks for a visible directory
choices.why: The dot is in the name ssh looks for.

prompt: Which `ls` option lists hidden names but leaves out `.` and `..`?
hint: A single letter, and it is the capital of the more familiar one.

prompt: Why does a `.tar.gz` have two extensions?
hint: Two separate operations were applied, in that order.

choices.text: Because tar writes a second index file beside the archive
choices.why: One file came out of it. The two names describe two steps applied to it.

choices.text: Because tar packed the files and gzip then shrank the result
choices.why: Right, and it is why gzip on its own takes a file rather than a directory.

choices.text: Because gzip needs the inner extension to pick its algorithm
choices.why: gzip has one algorithm, and it reads its own header rather than the name.

choices.text: Because the archive holds two formats and readers pick the newer
choices.why: There is one format inside, wrapped once.

prompt: In `tar -czf project.tar.gz src notes`, why does `f` have to come last among the letters?
hint: One of the letters takes a value.

choices.text: Because tar reads its letters from the right
choices.why: It reads them left to right, like any other option string.

choices.text: Because the compression letter has to be applied before the filename
choices.why: Order between c and z is free; what matters is which letter consumes a word.

choices.text: Because `f` consumes the next word as the archive's name
choices.why: Right, so `tar -cfz` would create an archive named `z`.

choices.text: Because `f` is a long option abbreviated to one letter
choices.why: It is an ordinary short option, and its behaviour is what matters here.

prompt: You have an archive from the internet and you do not know how it is laid out inside. What do you run before extracting?
hint: There is a letter for exactly this, and it changes nothing on disk.

choices.text: tar -tf archive.tar.gz
choices.why: Right, and it shows whether the paths sit inside one directory or scatter.

choices.text: tar -xf archive.tar.gz --dry-run
choices.why: tar has no such option, and the listing form already answers this.

choices.text: file archive.tar.gz
choices.why: That names the format, and says nothing about the paths inside.

choices.text: gzip -l archive.tar.gz
choices.why: That reports the compressed and uncompressed sizes, and no names.

prompt: You are sending a directory to a colleague on Windows. `tar` or `zip`?
hint: One of them opens with a double click over there; the other keeps things Linux cares about.

choices.text: tar, because it preserves permissions and ownership
choices.why: It does, and that is worth little on a machine that has no use for them.

choices.text: tar, because Windows has shipped a tar command since 2018
choices.why: It has, and your colleague still has to open a terminal to use it.

choices.text: Either — the two formats are equivalent in practice
choices.why: They differ in what they keep and in what opens them, which is the whole question.

choices.text: zip, because it opens with a double click there
choices.why: Right. Keep tar for what stays on Linux, where the modes matter.

prompt: `gzip -k draft.txt` produces a `.gz` that is larger than the original 20-byte file. Is that a bug?
hint: Compression is not free.

choices.text: Yes — gzip should leave a file alone when it would grow
choices.why: `gzip` on its own writes what it was asked to write; the archive tools do decline.

choices.text: No — the format's header outweighs what 20 bytes of text save
choices.why: Right, and it is why compression is worth measuring rather than assuming.

choices.text: No — the extra bytes are the original filename, kept for restoring it
choices.why: The name is stored, and it is a small part of a fixed overhead.

choices.text: Yes — the file was stored rather than compressed, which wastes the header
choices.why: Storing instead of deflating is a zip behaviour, and the header would still be needed.

prompt: Match each tar letter to its job.
hint: Three of them are the mode, and two are about the file.

prompt: You are in `/var/log/nginx`. Write the absolute path `../../lib` resolves to.
hint: Up two from nginx, then down into lib.

prompt: You are in `/home/ana`. Write the shortest relative path to `/home/bruno/notes.txt`.
hint: Up one, then down two.

prompt: A directory holds `a.txt`, `ab.txt`, `b.log` and `.hidden`. What does `echo ?.txt` print?
hint: The question mark stands for one character, and the star is not involved.

choices.text: a.txt
choices.why: Right — `ab.txt` has two characters before the dot, so it is out.

choices.text: a.txt ab.txt
choices.why: `ab.txt` would need two question marks to match.

choices.text: a.txt ab.txt b.log
choices.why: The pattern ends in `.txt`, which rules the log out.

choices.text: ?.txt
choices.why: It matched something, so the pattern was replaced rather than passed through.

prompt: In the same directory, what does `echo *` print?
hint: One of the four names is left out by a rule from section 45.

choices.text: a.txt ab.txt b.log .hidden
choices.why: The star does not match a leading dot, which is what keeps `rm *` survivable.

choices.text: a.txt ab.txt
choices.why: The star does not care about extensions; `b.log` matches it too.

choices.text: a.txt ab.txt b.log
choices.why: Right, and `.hidden` stays out because of its first character.
Three names matched, so the shell replaced the pattern with them.

prompt: Where does a machine's own configuration belong?
hint: It is text, and it is read rather than written while the machine runs.

choices.text: /usr/share
choices.why: Data that does not depend on the processor — icons, manuals, translations.

choices.text: /var/lib
choices.why: Working data a service writes while running.

choices.text: /opt
choices.why: A vendor's own tree, for software outside the package manager.

choices.text: /etc
choices.why: Right, and it is text, so a change is a diff somebody can read.

prompt: `ls -l secrets` prints `-rw-r--r-- 1 ana ana 0 Sep 14 09:00 secrets`. Is `secrets` a directory?
hint: One character answers it.

choices.text: Yes, and it is empty, which is why the size is 0
choices.why: An empty directory still reports 4096, and its line begins differently.

choices.text: No — the line begins with a dash
choices.why: Right, and a directory would show `d` and a link count of at least 2.

choices.text: Yes — the link count of 1 shows it is empty inside
choices.why: A directory's count starts at 2, because of its own `.` entry.

choices.text: There is no way to tell from a single long listing line
choices.why: The first character is the type, and it is there on every line.

prompt: You `rm` a 2 GB file and `df` shows no change. What is the most likely reason?
hint: Section 46's rule about names, and section 48's demonstration of it.

choices.text: A process still has the file open
choices.why: Right — `lsof` shows it with `(deleted)`, and the space returns when that process stops.

choices.text: The filesystem defers freeing until it needs the space
choices.why: ext4 frees blocks as the last reference goes, rather than on demand.

choices.text: df caches its answer for a few minutes
choices.why: It asks the filesystem each time it runs.

choices.text: The file was on a different filesystem from the one df reported on
choices.why: Worth checking, and the demonstration in section 48 ruled it out by using one path for both.

prompt: Write the command that lists the contents of `backup.tar.gz` without extracting anything.
hint: Three letters after the dash, and the f goes last.

prompt: A colleague's script writes to `logs/app.log` and runs from cron. Which change makes it dependable?
hint: A scheduled job starts in a directory nobody chose.

choices.text: Add `set -e` at the top so a failure stops the script
choices.why: Useful, and it does not change where a relative path lands.

choices.text: Run it more often so a missed write is caught sooner
choices.why: The writes are happening. They are landing somewhere unexpected.

choices.text: Write the path out in full, starting from the root
choices.why: Right — an absolute path means the same thing wherever the job begins.

choices.text: Add a `cd` into the project at the top of the script
choices.why: That works, and it puts the fix one line away from anybody who edits it later.

prompt: `find . -name '*.tmp' -delete` is about to run. What is the free check?
hint: The same command, minus one word.

choices.text: Add -maxdepth 1 so that it stays where it is
choices.why: That changes what is deleted rather than showing you what would be.

choices.text: Drop the last word and read the output
choices.why: Right: the printed list is exactly what the deletion would remove.

choices.text: Run it with sudo so no file is skipped
choices.why: That widens the reach, which is the opposite of a check.

choices.text: Add -type f so directories survive it
choices.why: Sensible, and it still does not show you the list first.

prompt: `ls -l /bin` shows one line and `ls -ld /bin/` shows another. What is the difference between the two commands?
hint: One of them goes through something.

choices.text: The second lists the contents and the first lists the entry
choices.why: Backwards: `-d` is what asks for the entry, and the second one has it.

choices.text: The second sorted its output and the first did not
choices.why: Sorting is the default in both, and one line each is what came out.

choices.text: The first was refused and fell back to describing the path
choices.why: Both succeeded. They described two different things.

choices.text: The trailing slash followed the symlink to the directory
choices.why: Right — with `-l` alone, ls describes the link rather than its target.

prompt: Put these in the order a careful person does them, before deleting a directory tree.
items: ls -d the path you are about to remove
read the listing and confirm it is the right tree
trap: Two checks come before the command, and one of them is about where you are standing.

prompt: Match each symptom to its cause.
hint: Each of the four was demonstrated in this lesson.

pairs.left: cat says No such file, ls shows the entry
pairs.right: a symlink whose target is gone

pairs.left: du and df disagree by gigabytes
pairs.right: a deleted file a process still holds open

pairs.left: a backup directory fills the root disk
pairs.right: nothing was mounted at the mount point
a pattern that matched nothing, passed through

right_distractors: a directory whose link count is 2

prompt: A file's `stat` shows Modify two years ago and Change an hour ago. What can you conclude?
hint: One timestamp covers more than the contents.

choices.text: Its metadata changed, and its contents did not
choices.why: Right — a rename, a chmod or a new owner moves ctime and leaves mtime alone.

choices.text: Somebody edited it an hour ago and reset the date
choices.why: Setting mtime backwards is possible, and it would move ctime too — which it did.

choices.text: It was read an hour ago
choices.why: Reading moves atime, which is the third line.

choices.text: The filesystem clock is wrong
choices.why: Two timestamps that differ are the normal case, not a symptom.

prompt: Write the redirect that throws a command's error messages away, leaving its results on screen.
hint: A number, an angle bracket, and a path from section 49.

prompt: `mv src dest` behaves differently depending on something not written on the line. What?
hint: The answer is about the destination.

choices.text: Whether src is a file or a directory
choices.why: A directory moves as one thing, and so does a file.

choices.text: Whether the two are on the same filesystem
choices.why: That changes the speed rather than the result.

choices.text: Whether dest exists as a directory
choices.why: Right: if it does, src lands inside it instead of becoming it.

choices.text: Whether you own dest
choices.why: Ownership decides if the move is refused, and not what it produces.
